objective: Plan incident response in platform engineering: on-call for the platform, runbooks, blameless reviews and error budgets shared with tenants
secondaryObjectives: DevOps practices in platform engineering: shared ownership, automation, feedback loops, and how a platform team serves product teams

The company, the platform, the tenant teams and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You facilitate a tabletop exercise for the internal platform team at Osprey Freight, a fictional logistics company. Thirty product teams run on the platform. The scenario: the shared ingress controller fails on a Monday morning and every tenant's public endpoints return errors.
handover: The platform has an on-call rotation but no incident commander role; tenants open tickets in their own queues.
The platform's SLO: 99.9% of ingress requests succeed each month.
howItWorks: The table shows the injects as they arrive, who is engaged, the communications and the decision log.
Move on a inject at a time. A decision comes to you at each inject; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Inject 2: two tenant teams roll back healthy releases, believing they caused the errors; one rollback reintroduces a fixed security bug.
Inject 3 (scenario): two months later the same certificate expires while the senior engineer is on leave; the outage lasts three hours.
The after-action note: in the next quarter, two near misses go unreported; engineers say they did not want to be named.

else.log: The exercise ends; the after-action report is due.

cmdPrompt.title: Who runs the incident?
cmdPrompt.context: The on-call platform engineer is debugging; 30 tenant teams are each opening tickets and debugging their own services.

choices.label: The platform declares the incident: an incident commander separate from the engineer fixing it, one status page and tenant channel, updates every 30 minutes

effects.log: The team names a commander and opens one channel.

choices.feedback: A shared capability's outage is the platform's incident: one commander, one channel, regular updates.

choices.label: The on-call engineer fixes it and answers tenant tickets as time allows

effects.log: The engineer works the fix and the tickets.

choices.feedback: The fix happens, but the engineer is split, and 30 teams wait on 30 queues.

choices.label: Fix it quietly; tenants will see it recover

effects.log: The team works with no announcement.

choices.feedback: Thirty teams spend the morning debugging their own healthy services.

runbookPrompt.title: No runbook for certificate expiry
runbookPrompt.context: The ingress controller's serving certificate expired; nobody knew how cert-manager renewed it, and the first fix attempt failed.

choices.label: Record the gap: a certificate-expiry runbook owned by the on-call lead by Friday, and an alert 21 days before any platform certificate expires

effects.log: The gap has an owner, a date and an alert.

choices.feedback: An exercise finds gaps; each needs an owner and a date, and automation where possible.

choices.label: Note 'write a runbook' in the exercise notes
choices.feedback: A gap without an owner and a date stays a gap.

choices.label: Decide the senior engineer who knows cert-manager will always handle it

effects.log: The senior engineer is the plan.

choices.feedback: The plan now depends on one person's memory and availability.

reviewPrompt.title: The review and the budget
reviewPrompt.context: The outage spent 38 minutes; the month's error budget is now exhausted. An executive asks who let the certificate expire.

choices.label: A blameless review of how the system allowed the expiry, action items with owners, and the error-budget policy applied: platform feature releases freeze for the month and reliability work comes first, shared with tenants

effects.log: Blameless review; budget policy applied and shared.

choices.feedback: Blameless reviews surface causes; an exhausted error budget shifts work to reliability, visibly to tenants.

choices.label: A blameless review, but keep releasing platform features this month
choices.feedback: Good learning, but the budget means nothing if spending it changes nothing.

choices.label: Name the engineer who set up the certificate in the report
choices.feedback: Blame teaches people to hide problems; the system that let the certificate expire is unchanged.

reflection.question: Write the after-action report: how the platform should run incidents in its shared capabilities, the gaps found with their owners, and how the error budget is used.

parts.label: Command and gaps
parts.criteria: A commander and one tenant channel; the runbook and expiry alert owned and dated.
parts.modelAnswer: The platform declares and commands incidents in shared capabilities, with one tenant channel. The certificate runbook and a 21-day expiry alert are owned by the on-call lead, due Friday.

parts.label: Learning and budget
parts.criteria: A blameless review; the exhausted budget freezes platform features for the month, shared with tenants.
parts.modelAnswer: The review looked at how the system let the certificate expire. The budget is spent, so platform releases pause for reliability work this month.

scoring.modelReasoning: A platform team owns incidents in the capabilities it provides: it declares them, separates the incident commander from the people fixing, and gives tenants one channel with regular updates. Exercises and incidents find gaps; each gets an owner, a date and automation where possible, not a hero. Reviews are blameless, and a shared error budget turns reliability into a policy: when it is spent, reliability work comes before features.
